You're using the privileged container, it means the files inside the container are owned by root. You're starting as user 1000, which means it cannot create new files within the space of the container.

For storage this isn't a problem, because you mount it externally. The storage directory is owned by user 1000.

There are two solutions to this:
1. use the `qdrant/qdrant:latest-unprivileged` container image
2. also mount `/qdrant/snapshots` to some directory where you control permissions, and set the owner to 1000

If both those approaches don't work you can run the container as root. But I don't recommend that.

query: Query filter returning empty result for a point in the collection
source_context:
Query filter returning empty result for a point in the collection

<!--- Provide a general summary of the issue in the Title above -->
target:
The recommended approach is to insert points **after** creating payload indices, yes. That way you're sure the payload indices are used to enrich the HNSW graph, resulting in better search accuracy.

With some effort, you can recreate the HNSW indices without having to recreate the whole collection. You may temporarily [update](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/collections/#update-collection-parameters) the collection and set the HNSW `m` parameter to 0. Once the collection is done optimizing you can set it back to the original value. Once it is done optimizing a second time you should see improved search results.

Supersedes <https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/pull/7341> based on [this](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/pull/7341#issuecomment-3370505121) comment.

I'd argue that this is the better implementation of <https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/pull/7341>. Please see my motivation [here](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/pull/7341#issuecomment-3370505121).

I also argue this is better than <https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/pull/7342> because this is cheaper. Snapshots are already very expensive, flushing them makes this worse. We already have a background task that is supposed to take care of this.

After another pass, I agree that <https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/pull/7342> is the better approach.

The force flush in each segment on snapshot should not be a concern.

Leaving the queue proxy as-is is fine. In case of snapshot transfer, we instantiate it before doing all flushes. All flushes are forced, and use a plunger to ensure parallel operations are also properly flushed.

Closing this in favor of <https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/pull/7342>.

query: Implement RAM and Disk usage computation for collection statistics
source_context: Implement RAM and Disk usage computation for collection statistics
target:
Hi, thanks for the contribution!
Disk usage implementation looks good to me.

But I can see some potential difficulties with RAM estimation. I assume you were trying to estimate memory usage precisely, but as I understood from my research - it might be almost impossible to do. Some data structures have internal memory usage which could not be directly estimated.
Second point is that even if we could estimate all individual payloads and vectors - it would require us to traverse the whole collection, which might require a significant amount of time. And I would like this API to be executed in constant time.

The other solution is to estimate memory approximately.
Possible approaches I would like to try are:
1. Estimate memory consumption of vector storage by just multiplying `NumOfVectors x vectorSize x sizeof(f32)`
2. Estimate payload memory usage by `NumberOfRecords x coef`, where coef is determined from used disk space
3. Estimate indexes memory usage by `UsedDiskSize x coef`.

In this scenario `coef` is an experimental value, and it is not obvious if this method would ever be reliable.


In this context, I would like to propose that only the changes relating to disk size in this PR should be retained. So I could merge it and we could discuss the RAM usage calculation separately.

query: Feature Request: Truncate API
source_context:
Feature Request: Truncate API

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
When implementing and testing features, it's often necessary to delete and recreate data. However, qdrant doesn't have this feature, so the quickest way is to delete the table and then recreate it.
However, this is quite cumbersome. It would be nice to have a feature that could solve this problem.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add a "truncate" API to remove all data from a specific collection.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
none

**Additional context**
none
target:
I don't think we can implement something much more efficient than delete by filter. Note that it's already quite optimized when used with a payload index.

Another possibility may be to use custom sharding. You'd put points in a specific named shard, and you can drop such shard with a single API call. It will be quite similar to dropping the whole collection, but allows you to use some partitioning.
Docs: https://qdrant.tech/documentation/guides/distributed_deployment/#user-defined-sharding

Since I don't think we have a more optimized 'large delete by filter' or 'truncate' API call planned I'm closing this.

Thanks for the suggestion!

Abort pending blocking search tasks when we drop/invalidate the search

Critical fix for large clusters with huge search load.

Searches spawn blocking search tasks on a dedicated thread pool. The pool size is limited, and so these search tasks may be queued. If there is a humongous amount of incoming searches, this queue may get infinitely long.

When a search is invalidated (timed out, or completed through fan out), we drop the async task. The idea is that we abort all work related to this search to release resources.

It turns out that these spawned tasks will always remain queued and will be run to completion, even if the owning future was already dropped and aborted. Instead, we must explicitly cancel these pending spawned blocking tasks.

Luckily tokio provides us the [`AbortOnDropHandle`](https://docs.rs/tokio-util/latest/tokio_util/task/struct.AbortOnDropHandle.html) utility, which is what I've implemented in this PR.

On a huge cluster that accumulate a massive amount of pending searches, it was possible to keep segments busy for more than an hour. Even though each search itself might only be a few seconds of work. This can break optimizations if they cannot release old segments for over an hour. This PR will help prevent this issue from happening by cancelling all invalidated searches early. More specifically, it helps prevent this error from happening:

```
Service internal error: Removing proxy segment which is still in use
```
target:
Correct.

We can add a test for it, but I'd consider that obsolete. Because then we'd be testing tokio fundamentals. [`spawn_`](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/task/fn.spawn_blocking.html) functions are intended to keep the task even if the caller is dropped. It was simply an oversight from our side when implementing this.

query: Fix abort resharding live-lock
source_context:
Fix abort resharding live-lock

We are testing shard-holder live-lock during scale-down resharding abort.

- while applying update, we **hold shard-holder read-lock**
- when consensus marks `ReshardingScaleDown` node as `Dead`, it aborts resharding
  - when aborting resharding, we need to briefly **acquire write-lock to shard-holder**
- when updates to *multiple* shards land in right order, it is possible to have a live-lock, because
  - update holds shard-holder read-lock
  - at the same time, consensus tries to abort resharding, which tries to write-lock shard-holder
  - but update also **waits for abort resharding consensus operation to resolve**
  - which locks consensus operation, because update holds shard-holder read-lock...
  - fortunately, there's a timeout when update is waiting for consensus, so everything unblocks after 30 seconds

So, currently, we expect *last line* in the test (`upsert_random_points`) to fail with a timeout.

On my machine, the test is 80-90% reliable. It _sometimes_ gives false-positive (passes, even though the bug is present), but 4 out of 5 runs fails as expected. It's timing related, not sure how to make it completely deterministic. 😬

query: Performance issue with prefetch + multivector reranking
source_context:
Performance issue with prefetch + multivector reranking

I’m trying to use ColBERT embeddings in Qdrant because, in my experience, they provide by far the best retrieval accuracy. I’m following the recommended two-stage approach: prefetching with a single-vector embedding and then reranking using MaxSim.

**Collection definition:**

```python
client.create_collection(
    collection_name=self.collection_name,
    vectors_config={
        "dense": models.VectorParams(
            size=1024,
            distance=models.Distance.DOT
        ),
        "colbert": models.VectorParams(
            size=128,
            distance=models.Distance.DOT,
            multivector_config=models.MultiVectorConfig(
                comparator=models.MultiVectorComparator.MAX_SIM
            ),
            hnsw_config=models.HnswConfigDiff(m=0)  # Disable HNSW for reranking
        )
    }
)
```

**Search operations:**

```python
search_params = models.SearchParams(
    hnsw_ef=hnsw_ef,
    acorn=models.AcornSearchParams(
        enable=True,
        max_selectivity=self.acorn_max_selectivity,
    )
)

prefetch = [
    models.Prefetch(
        query=dense_query,
        using="dense",
        limit=prefetch_limit,
        filter=query_filter,
        params=search_params
    )
]

results: QueryResponse = self.client.query_points(
    collection_name=self.collection_name,
    prefetch=prefetch,
    query=colbert_query,
    using="colbert",
    limit=top_k,
    with_payload=True
)
```

The issue is that search becomes extremely slow, but only once a sufficient amount of data has been indexed. I’ve experimented with various parameters (e.g. `ef`, ACORN settings, prefetch limits, different disk IOPS configurations), but none of these changes had a dramatic impact on performance.

The Qdrant data directory is currently around 100 GB. With smaller datasets, I did not observe this problem.

I ran several ablation experiments to isolate the cause:

1. Searching only with the single-vector embedding (while still storing the multivector data) — performance is still equally slow.
2. Using two separate collections, one for single-vector embeddings and one for ColBERT embeddings — still slow.
3. Using two separate Qdrant instances on two different servers — this works as expected.

My current hypothesis is that the way multivector embeddings are stored negatively impacts prefetch performance, even when the ColBERT vectors are not actively used during the prefetch stage. This suggests a potential issue with storage layout or data locality.
target:
Hey @agoriwmt, thanks for the feedback and experiments.

Based on your observations, the best hypothesis I can think of - cache memory saturation. As far as I can see from your configuration, both dense and multi vectors are stored with default parameters for memory location ( which is `on_disk=false`). That means both dense and multi vectors are loaded into RAM on start. If there is not enough room, qdrant doesn't fail, but evicts part of the data from RAM, which can cause extra disk requests during query time.

I propose the following experiments to confirm/reject this hypothesis:

- Searching only with the single-vector embedding (while still storing the multivector data), but enable `"on_disk": true` option for multivectors.

- Search with prefetch and rescore, but enable scalar quantization for dense vectors. Quantized vectors in qdrant do not use mmaps, so they can't be evicted from RAM.

Alternatively, I can propose a help from our solution architects, to achieve best configuration for your specific use-case.

Please let me know results of the experiments and if you would like to talk to Sales.

query: [rocksdb] Investigate compression scheme for RocksDB
source_context:
[rocksdb] Investigate compression scheme for RocksDB

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
A quick profiling session on a heavy write workload shows that Snappy can take up to 2% of CPU time.
![snappy](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/606963/178513624-622407d2-c69f-49d8-83e8-58237b5a3a02.png)

The official doc says:

```
Use options.compression to specify the compression to use.
By default it is Snappy. We believe LZ4 is almost always better than Snappy.
```
https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb/wiki/Compression

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Investigate if it can be beneficial to switch to another compression scheme.

e.g.

```rust
options.set_compression_type(DBCompressionType::Lz4);
```
target:
We are aware of capacity allocations in our code base. In many where it makes sense we control this and limit growing. Generally speaking, this only makes sense for long lived data structures.

But, we don't use `shrink_to_fit()` very often because this can be very inefficient. Instead you should prevent growing your capacity when it's not needed.

In many data structures we still want mutability to add new entries at any time. If you'd always use exact capacity here, with `reserve_exact()` or `shrink_to_fit()` for example, you always need to reallocate for every new insertion which is very costly.


So, this is for good reason.

A lot of data types we have that are not mutable, already have their exact capacity set.

By the way, if you have a specific point in code where this happens, please ( :pray: ) feel free to point at it. Then we can discuss and improve.

query: UIO: add flag to preserve callback order in `read_batch`
source_context:
UIO: add flag to preserve callback order in `read_batch`

I plan to implement an iterator interface on top of `UniversalRead`.
Particularly, I want to implement the [`FallibleIterator::try_fold`](https://docs.rs/fallible-iterator/latest/fallible_iterator/trait.FallibleIterator.html#method.try_fold) method.

To do so, I need to adjust `read_batch` to let it call callbacks items in order.
This PR adds an additional generic parameter `YieldOrder` to force strict ordering.

For `io_uring` implementation, the strict ordering is achieved by using the new ringbuf-like structure that holds items that completed out of sequence. The same structure can be reused later for S3 or other async implementations.

Also, this PR adds a generic error parameter `E` to `read_batch` to let it fit into the `try_fold` interface. (and I think this approach is more idiomatic anyway)

For future reference and #support:

The following operations _may_ trigger this red status:

* create payload index (`PUT /collections/{collection_name}/index`)
* delete payload index (`DELETE /collections/{collection_name}/index/{name}`)
* update collection parameters (`PATCH /collections/{collection_name}`)

If a collection currently has a red status caused by this, these are the options from best to worst:

* upgrade to 1.18.0+, the issue cannot happen again
  (may need to [re-trigger optimizers](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/manage-data/collections/#grey-collection-status) after restart to get rid of grey status)
* restart the node having red status and [re-trigger optimizers](https://qdrant.tech/documentation/manage-data/collections/#grey-collection-status), don't use above operations until upgrade
* if replicated, copy other shards onto the shards having red status (costly)
* ignore the problem and keep red status, will result in a very unoptimized collection (causing slow searches and excess data usage) and a fragile deployment

In 1.18.0+ this issue cannot happen again. It also implements [this](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/pull/8767) which allows to drop the red status without a restart by updating collection parameters.

query: fix: segment merge tolerates source missing a named vector
source_context:
fix: segment merge tolerates source missing a named vector

Optimization fails with `Cannot update from other segment because it is missing vector name X` when the optimizer merges a segment whose schema lags the collection's.

  ## Cause

  `create_vector_name` propagates V to every segment alive at dispatch time, but
  nothing stops a concurrent optimizer job from outliving the schema change:

  1. Optimizer job J starts. Captures `target_config` from the pre-change schema.
  2. `create_vector_name(V)` runs. Every loaded segment receives V.
     `recreate_optimizers_blocking()` refreshes the cached config for *future*
     jobs but does not cancel J.
  3. J finishes with the old `target_config` and installs a merged segment C
     with no V. C inherits `max(source versions)` — too high for the older
     `CreateVectorName` op_num to retroactively apply (`handle_segment_version`).
  4. The next optimizer job uses the refreshed `target_config = {…, V}`, picks
     C as a source, and fails: `C.vector_data` has no entry for V.

  ## Fix

  Make `SegmentBuilder::update` tolerate sources missing a target named vector,
  matching the "no data for V" state `create_vector_name` records on existing
  points:

  - `BatchedVectorReader::source_vector_storages` → `&[Option<AtomicRef>]`;
    missing sources emit a typed placeholder with `deleted = true`.
  - Skip `old_indices` push for missing sources (HNSW reuse only cares about
    present indices).
  - Skip quantization training when `available_vector_count() == 0` — otherwise
    PQ k-means / SQ scale-fit hits all-deleted data.

  Patches the merge boundary; the underlying race with in-flight optimization is
  unchanged.
target:
As I understand it this data race happens because we take a collection config and proxy segments to optimize, but these don't happen at the same time. Updating the named vector configuration can fall in between.

I wonder if it makes sense to serialize these two processes. Though I don't like another lock, I do believe it would work here. Maybe there's a similar trick we can use here. Doesn't that make this behavior of segments mismatching the collection config entirely impossible?

I'm not saying we should not use the current implementation, I'd just like to discuss this other approach for a bit.

query: facet: bound per-shard response size with over-fetched top-k
source_context: facet: bound per-shard response size with over-fetched top-k
target:
Good question — taken in isolation, `LocalShard::approx_facet` could compute its own cap as `limit * over_fetch`. The reason `output_limit` exists as a separate parameter is what happens at node boundaries; `limit` and "max hits this hop is allowed to return" are not the same value:

1. **Different semantics.** `limit` is the user's final result size (it has to travel end-to-end so the coordinator knows how many rows to return). `output_limit` is the per-shard cap chosen by the coordinator. Inferring one from the other forces every level to bake in the over-fetch policy.

2. **Configurability lives in one place.** Today `FACET_OVER_FETCH_FACTOR` is a constant in `Collection::facet`, but a follow-up could easily make it adaptive (e.g. depend on the number of shards, or be tunable per request). Shards just obey the cap the coordinator hands them — they don't need to know the policy.

3. **Rolling-upgrade correctness.** This is the important one. `top_k` is wire-`optional`. When an **old coordinator** talks to a **new node**, the new node sees no `top_k`, falls back to "return all hits" (legacy behavior), and the old coordinator's cross-shard merge stays correct. If a new node instead inferred its cap from `limit`, an old coordinator would silently get per-shard truncation it doesn't expect — and the per-shard `top_hits(_, limit)` call already in `Collection::facet` was exactly the latent correctness bug this PR fixes (values low in one shard but high in the global sum got dropped).

So even though `output_limit = limit * factor` is the value the coordinator picks today, treating it as a first-class parameter is what lets us (a) change the policy in one place, (b) skip per-shard caps when an upstream caller did its own over-fetch already (`exact=true`, or another internal handler), and (c) stay compatible during mixed-version upgrades.

Happy to add a doc comment to `ShardOperation::facet` making this contract explicit if it helps.

query: Enable multivector in Collection model test, fix multi-dense reload corruption
source_context: Enable multivector in Collection model test, fix multi-dense reload corruption
target:
I feel like we're looking at a different problem, which needs a different solution.

These are the flush steps, in flush order:

1. vector bytes (mmap)
2. vector status (total length)
3. offset bytes (mmap)
4. offset status (total length)
5. delete flags

The statuses are used when new data is written to the files. It defines the offset in the file at which to append new entries.

Isn't the root problem that we flush the offset bytes out of bound? Specifically, that offset bytes are durably stored before the vector status is durably stored?

It looks like we don't buffer offset updates like we do in other storages (such as Gridstore). Because we currently put them in a memory map directly, the kernel might flush them for us at any point in time.

Once we get into a state where offsets are already persisted but the vector status file is not persisted yet, WAL replay breaks. When WAL replay updates a multi vector, it will start writing the new vector bytes from the (stale) persisted offset. It will overwrite any bytes that already exist in that place and it will corrupt multi vectors pointing to that range.

I feel like buffering offset updates will fix the issue. It will make sure that we never have any offsets durably stored pointing to bytes after the persisted vector status file. We only have to buffer offset changes until flush, we don't have to buffer vector byte changes.

source_context:
Number of results

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
It's always useful, when using score_threshold, to anticipate how many results there will be.

Add an option to return the number of results (or at least an estimate or a max vlaue, I understand there might be some performances impact with HNSW)

target:
Hi!

We received this request multiple times, but unfortunately didn't find a suitable technical solution for the problem:

- Vector index doesn't provide any information about the count of records by any other means except for actually retrieving the vectors. It makes counting operation almost as expensive as the search itself, moreover, search with very high limit.
- Even if we will use exact counting to the `score_threshold`, the number of points may increase by order of magnitude with just a small change of the score_threshold parameter.

The combination of this 2 factors makes this function unstable and potentially dangerous for production use case.

We are happy to reconsider as soon as there will be a way to provide number estimation avoiding the actual retrieval of the vectors

query: Feature request: Evaluation of Approaches for Enabling BM25 Scoring on Existing Payload Fields
source_context:
Feature request: Evaluation of Approaches for Enabling BM25 Scoring on Existing Payload Fields

Motivation: If users have already imported a large amount of data, enabling BM25 scoring on existing Payload fields without re-importing the data can save manpower and various costs incurred during the data re-import process.

The current process for enabling BM25 on an existing Payload field is:

1. The user updates the collection configuration and adds a sparse vector field.
2. The user externally re-imports the Payload field that already exists in the Collection into the corresponding sparse vector field.

This introduces a problem:

- If the data volume is large, the cost of the entire process is close to importing another full copy of the data.

target:
Hey @TY0909 thanks for suggestion.

Let me provide some initial feedback on the proposal. Feel free to adjust or argue ;)



Background processes are notoriously hard to make consistent and stable. The amount of machinery we have to involve to make optimizers stable enough is enourmous, and we still keep finding edge cases. Having another background worker system will make it exponentially worse.



This option is better than the previous one, but still doesn't allign well with our architecture.

In Qdrant, there is a clear boundary between "input data" and "vectors". Embedding inference happens before we even write anything into WAL, and after that only vectors exist.
Involving optimizer into this process will break this boundary and leak embedding mechanisms into segment level.

On top of that, it seems that proposed approach puts bm25 as some form of exception over other embedding models. Our vision is not aligned with that. We only have bm25 inside the core as an exception because it is simple enough and popular enough to be implemented in the core. But in a long run we prefer to not enlarge this exception.




This is the most aligned approach with our vision - to introduce the scroing capability along with filtering.
Most of all, it will require re-design of the query interface, but I can see how this approach might just pay off.

If we going to go this way, it will require much more detailed design document.


I hope my feedback makes sense, please let me know what you are thinking

Please describe.** After a hard node crash (power loss) on a single-node Qdrant 1.18.2, several shards' appendable segments had Gridstore-backed payload index blobs torn mid-flush. On every startup, loading the first affected map index panics deep in the deserializer: ``` ERROR qdrant::startup: Panic occurred in file lib/gridstore/src/blob.rs at line 25: Failed to deserialize Vec<ecow::EcoString>: ErrorImpl { code: Message("invalid type: integer `0`, expected a sequence"), offset: 0 } ERROR qdrant::startup: Panic occurred in file lib/collection/src/shards/replica_set/mod.rs at line 312: Failed to load local shard "./storage/collections/<collection>/24": ... ``` A second shard failed with a different flavor of the same problem (truncated blob): ``` Failed to deserialize Vec<ecow::EcoString>: ErrorImpl { code: EofWhileParsingValue, offset: 0 } ``` The result is a permanent crash loop of the whole node. With a 32-shard collection that takes ~35 min to load, each corrupt shard discovered costs another full crash cycle. `storage.handle_collection_load_errors=true` doesn't help beyond making the node boot — it marks the entire shard as a dummy (unavailable for reads *and* writes), with no rebuild. Storage was a local filesystem (no "Unrecognized filesystem" warning), so this is not the unsupported-FS case from #7610 — any power loss during a Gridstore flush can produce this. **Describe the solution you'd like** Treat a payload index that fails to *deserialize* the same as one that is *missing*: `StructPayloadIndex::load_from_db` already sets a rebuild flag when an index fails to load and rebuilds it from payload storage (`Rebuilding payload index for field ...`). If `MapIndex::new_gridstore` / the Gridstore open path returned `Ok(None)` (or a recoverable error mapped to the rebuild path) on deserialization failure, the existing machinery would self-heal on startup with zero data loss, since payload storage is the source of truth. **Describe alternatives you've considered** - `handle_collection_load_errors=true` — node boots, but the shard is a dummy: no reads, no writes, no rebuild. - Manual recovery (what we did, successfully): identify the corrupt segment from `QDRANT__LOG_LEVEL=debug` field-load lines, then move all field index dirs out of that segment's `payload_index/` (keeping `config.json`). On next load Qdrant logs `Rebuilding payload
target:
After some investigation, Longhorn may be the problem here.

Longhorn v1.12 does not appear to support a flush operation. To alternatively, writes would only be safe if an acknowledged write means it will be durable. But Longhorn does not guarantee that.

Other factors may make this much worse. For example, if write caching is enabled on the machine that hosts those HDDs there is a much larger crash window. Could you validate whether this is enabled on your Longhorn setup?

The power loss event probably broke storage here. Qdrant writes data to Longhorn, it cannot flush, and Longhorn simply hopes its volatile data is written to disk in time. If not, it's lost.

I confirmed once again that the write path in Qdrant is sound. It is strictly ordered, making the situation you're seeing impossible on a stable file system which can be durably flushed.

I'm afraid the only real solution is to switch to a file system that can be reliably flushed. Otherwise it's a matter of waiting for another crash to happen.

query: Recover from appendable segment overflow (core + replica resilience) (#9158)
source_context:
Recover from appendable segment overflow (core + replica resilience) (#9158)

Split out of #9906 (part 1 of 2). This is the complete, correct fix for #9158; the inline update-worker retry is layered on top in the stacked follow-up.

Filter-based payload/vector operations CoW-move points from immutable segments into an appendable segment with no size check, growing it far past `max_segment_size` (#9158). Instead of provisioning capacity inside the update path, the update fails recoverably and reuses the machinery around it:

1. The update path filters CoW-move destinations and upsert targets to appendable segments under the configured cap, checked once per batch. When none is under the cap, the operation fails with the recoverable `OutOfAppendableCapacity` error (its producer, until now inert).
2. The error maps to a transient shard-unavailable failure, so the collection updater queues it in `failed_operation`, pinning the WAL acknowledge: the operation survives restarts.
3. The update worker wakes the optimizer on transient failures. The optimizer wake-up ensures an under-cap appendable segment exists (creating one if not) and runs failed-operation recovery, which re-applies the operation; already-applied points are skipped by version, exactly like WAL replay.
4. An operation moving more data than one segment holds fails again after filling the fresh segment; the wake-up re-signals itself to provision the next one, progress-guarded so an empty segment stops the chain.

**Replica resilience:** a replica or leader that runs out of appendable capacity self-heals via the recovery above, so it is not deactivated over that condition; deactivating would force a full transfer to recover a replica that catches up on its own. The condition is recognized both locally and when reported by a remote replica over gRPC.
target: Closing: splitting the inline retry out (see #9971) breaks client-visible write semantics — CI rust-tests fail because ordinary writes return a transient ShardUnavailable on capacity exhaustion. The core and the inline retry are coupled; shipping as the single PR #9906 instead.

query:
Also, some explanation for the changes.

_For some reason_, we decided to return 0 (which means "ignore cluster commit check"), if we did not get *at least* `required_commit_indices_count` successful responses... which is silly?

Unless someone somehow *manually* break the cluster in some elaborate way (e.g., modified node data on disk, or added a node from *another* cluster to the existing one), getting *any* consensus commit is better than getting none:

- Maybe we get consensus commit from an *even more* outdated node (which is only possible in 4+ nodes cluster, btw), but then it's just the same as before.
- If we get consensus commit from a *slightly* outdated node, then maybe we won't *perfectly* synchronize with consensus, but it's still better, than doing no synchronization at all.
- And, of course, we might get lucky and get consensus commit from an up-to-date node.

So I removed this nonsense logic, and I always return `max` of *any* commit indices we have. We only return 0 if *all* requests failed.

I don't think we can just remove the directory. The replica (local shard) must exist, because consensus tells us it should.

If we just remove the directory, we must remove the replica from consensus (and confirm that, which is not trivial).

You make a good point though. Just removing the initialized file here may be incorrect, because another crash will not get it into the same state on restart.

I think we must do either of:
- load dummy shard, mark shard as dead (if not done already), confirm with consensus, only then remove initialized file
- remove replica entirely, confirm with consensus, remove directory

I strongly prefer the first, because I see two more problems with the second approach:
- we might accidentally remove the last  replica of some shard
- we lose the replica set state, which we should always have, even if not having a local replica

query:
The scoped thread here does not make sense. Because we join it, it'll always block the current thread for the lifetime of the spawned thread. The idea that spawning a thread here will unblock the current (drop) runtime is not correct. Spawning the extra thread is therefore obsolete. In this case, we can just run `self.blocking_ask_workers_to_stop()` directly on our current thread.

Also, this still has the potential to deadlock if we lock `update_handler` through other means. So this only shifts the problem.

For example, we will deadlock again if:
- we run on 1 CPU
- we yield the thread at one of these await points: https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/blob/28112fdffa7e393d76c9d38e6a843ae2e91e42bf/lib/collection/src/shards/local_shard/updaters.rs#L64-L67
- we run `on_optimizer_config_update` and implicit `drop` on same runtime

I'd argue assuming that won't happen, or trying our best to not run these on the same runtime is not good enough.

Instead I think the only right way to solve this is to:
- still externally stop it gracefully first (like in this PR)
- make this drop handler not block (nor join) at all
- use an atomic bool or other lock free structure to probe status, print an error if not stopped
- if not stopped, stop it asynchronously (stop msg through channel?)

I've yet to validate whether this is easily doable.

target:
While we didn't come up with a perfect solution for this, it is much better now.

Under normal circumstances - when `stop_gracefully` is correctly called - drop does not block anymore and shortcuts early.

In cases where we forgot the shard workers will be cancelled asynchronously.

This means that all places that depend on releasing everything need to call ``stop_gracefully().await`. This has been implemented across the code base.
